title: Does Your Organization Track a Proprietary Metric? Date Published: June 3, 2026 Original URL: https://admiredleadership.substack.com
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that the best organizations go beyond common dashboards to develop proprietary metrics — unique predictive indicators that competitors overlook, that reveal underlying root causes, and that change how leaders see performance. The article distinguishes between standard metrics (revenue, margin, customer satisfaction, team engagement — common to virtually all organizations) and proprietary metrics that are unique to a specific organization's strategic insight about what actually drives its outcomes. Four case studies illustrate the concept: Airbnb's 'magic moments' metric for repeat bookings, Netflix's completion-and-retention data by show, Amazon's customer lifetime value calculations, and Toyota's Jidoka ratio measuring the frequency with which workers stop the line to fix defects. Costco's adoption of sales-per-square-foot as a north star metric before competitors recognized its predictive power is cited as an example of proprietary insight that became industry standard once its value was apparent. The article's practical challenge to leaders is to work backward from outcomes to root causes until they find a measure of something that predicts future performance and that almost no one else is measuring — a process that requires deep understanding of one's own operational mechanics. The best proprietary metrics are counterintuitive: they often measure something others dismiss, track root causes rather than outcomes, and give leaders the ability to see around corners before the effects are visible in standard dashboards.
points: Standard metrics like revenue growth, customer satisfaction, and team engagement are necessary but insufficient: because competitors track the same things, they offer no strategic advantage, and because they measure outcomes rather than drivers, they reveal what happened rather than what will happen.

Toyota's Jidoka ratio inverts the usual incentive: a higher rate of workers stopping the production line is a positive metric, because it measures both the willingness to surface problems and the organizational capacity to fix root causes rather than pass defects downstream.

Airbnb's 'magic moments' metric exemplifies the behavioral analysis approach: rather than measuring satisfaction (an outcome), it measured the specific interactions that cause repeat bookings (a behavioral driver), which is more predictive and more actionable.

The counterintuitive quality of great proprietary metrics is by design: if the metric were obvious, competitors would already be using it, and its predictive power would already be priced into the competitive landscape.

The practical process for finding a proprietary metric begins with asking what the single most important root cause of future performance is that standard dashboards don't show — and then being willing to invest in measuring it, even if it's hard to measure.
quotes: To assess the health and productivity of their teams and organizations, leaders create, measure, and rely on key metrics. The scorecards, dashboards, and financial reviews used at most organizations focus on many of the same indicators.

But the best organizations go further, examining everything they can, looking for a predictive metric that others overlook or haven't thought of. When they find a metric that adds tremendous value, they consider it proprietary to the organization.

Toyota's production system tracks the rate of Jidoka — the practice that empowers workers to stop the line when they detect defects and then fix the root cause. For Toyota, a higher Jidoka ratio is the best reflection of quality.

The best metrics are proprietary in nature as they remain largely unknown to other organizations. They predict future outcomes and are often counterintuitive or measure something others dismiss or overlook.
The best metric is the one that allows you to see around corners. Data is common. Knowing what metric changes everything is rare and worth finding.
